items.text: \operatorname{Ker}F_G\ \text{represented by}\ k[t_{ij}][\Delta^{-1}]\big/\bigl(t_{ij}^p\ (i\ne j),\ t_{ii}^p-1\bigr);\quad \lambda_{ii}^p=1\iff(\lambda_{ii}-1)^p=0

Non-commutative; infinitesimal (in a reduced ring $\lambda_{ij}=0$, $\lambda_{ii}=1$) but not trivial as soon as $k'$ has nilpotents. $F_G$ is an epimorphism (in the sense of sheaves): $G$ is the quotient of $G$ by this infinitesimal subgroup.
Diagonalisable groups $D(M)$
$M$ an abelian group:
D(M)\colon k'\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}\bigl(M,\,k'^{*}\bigr)\qquad(\text{contravariant in }M)
D(\mathbb Z)=\mathbb G_m,\qquad D(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)=\mu_n
$M$ of finite type, $M=\bigoplus M_i$ with $M_i\simeq\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb Z/n$: $D(M)=\prod D(M_i)$, a group of finite type.
General $M$: need a universal homomorphism of $M$ into the multiplicative group of a $k$-algebra — the group algebra.
k[M]=\bigoplus_{m\in M}k\,e^m,\qquad e^m e^{m'}=e^{m+m'}
$k[M]$ commutative if $M$ is. Maps $M\to k'$ (multiplicative) correspond to $k$-algebra maps $k[M]\to k'$:
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(M,k'^{*})=\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(k[M],k'),\qquad D(M)\ \text{represented by}\ k[M]
M=\mathbb Z:\ k[M]=k[t,t^{-1}]
Diagonalisable groups: for $M$ of finite type these are the groups embeddable in a group of diagonal matrices, i.e. in $\mathbb G_m^{\,r}$ (over a field).
Radicial (infinitesimal) groups
A group functor $G$ is radicial (= infinitesimal) if $G(k')=\{1\}$ for every reduced $k'$ over $k$. Examples: $\mu_p$, $\alpha_p$, the kernel of Frobenius.
Over a field of characteristic $0$ a radicial algebraic group is trivial (not proved).
$D(M)$ as a Hom functor
D(M)=\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\text{gr}}\bigl(M_k,\mathbb G_m\bigr),\qquad M_k\colon k'\mapsto M\ \text{(constant functor)}
D(M)\times M_k\to\mathbb G_m,\qquad M_k\to\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}\bigl(D(M),\mathbb G_m\bigr)\ \ (\text{essentially an isomorphism})
Group laws in terms of the algebra
$X\leftrightarrow A$; $X\times X\leftrightarrow A\otimes A$; a composition law $X\times X\to X$ is a $k$-algebra homomorphism (comultiplication):
\pi\colon A\to A\otimes A
An action $X\times Y\to Y$, $Y\leftrightarrow B$: a homomorphism $B\to A\otimes B$.
Associativity. $X\times X\times X\rightrightarrows X\times X\to X$ commutes; dually:
\begin{CD} A @>{\pi}>> A\otimes A\\ @V{\pi}VV @VV{\pi\otimes 1}V\\ A\otimes A @>{1\otimes\pi}>> A\otimes A\otimes A \end{CD}
Unit. A section of $X$ over the final object $e$ = an augmentation $\varepsilon\colon A\to k$.
X\xrightarrow{\ (\varepsilon,1)\ }X\times X\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }X\ \ =\ \mathrm{id}\ (\text{left unit});\qquad (1,\varepsilon)\ \text{for the right unit}

A\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }A\otimes A\xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon\otimes 1\ }k\otimes A=A\ =\ \mathrm{id}_A,\qquad A\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }A\otimes A\xrightarrow{\ 1\otimes\varepsilon\ }A\otimes k=A\ =\ \mathrm{id}_A
$\varepsilon$ is unique if it exists (the counit).
Commutativity. With the symmetry $s\colon x\otimes y\mapsto y\otimes x$ of $A\otimes A$:
s\circ\pi=\pi
Inverse
There is $\sigma\colon X\to X$ with $g\,\sigma(g)=1$:
X\xrightarrow{\ (1,\sigma)\ }X\times X\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }X\ =\ X\to e\xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon\ }X
A\xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }A\otimes A\xrightarrow{\ 1\otimes\sigma\ }A\otimes A\xrightarrow{\ x\otimes y\mapsto xy\ }A\ =\ A\xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon\ }k\to A
$\sigma\colon A\to A$ a $k$-algebra homomorphism (the "contraposition"); unique when it exists.
Coalgebras

$\pi\colon A\to A\otimes A$ is a comultiplication; it is associative (diagram 1), commutative (diagram 2), unitary if there is an augmentation $\varepsilon\colon A\to k$ making diagram 3 commute (counit, unique).
These notions make sense for a bare $k$-module $A$: a coalgebra structure = an associative unitary comultiplication $\pi$.
